title: Experts React: Takeaways from President Trump’s Trip to Asia
text:
Experts React: Takeaways from President Trump’s Trip to Asia

Photo: Kremlin Press Service/Anadolu/Getty Images

Commentary
by

Edgard D. Kagan,

Gregory B. Poling,

Bonny Lin,

Thomas J. Christensen,

Brian Hart,

Joseph Rodgers,

Thomas Glynn Hanley,

Aman Thakker,

Romina Bandura,

J. Stephen Morrison,
and
Michaela Simoneau

Published November 20, 2026

This week, President Donald Trump traveled to Asia to attend a busy schedule of leader-level events: the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and a Quad leaders’ summit in Manila, and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit and a trilateral meeting with Presidents Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. Experts from across CSIS react to the trip, discussing what happened at these events and how the meetings might impact U.S. relations with China, Russia, and the Indo-Pacific going forward.

Table of Contents

Shenzhen APEC Trip: Munich Without Umbrellas—or Paper—Not Yalta 2.0 | Edgard D. Kagan
Trump in Manila: Symbolism over Substance | Gregory B. Poling

Takeaways from the Trilateral Summit’s Joint Statement | Thomas J. Christensen
Xi Gets a Boost | Brian Hart

Image

Shenzhen APEC Trip: Munich Without Umbrellas—or Paper—Not Yalta 2.0Edgard D. Kagan, Freeman Chair in China Studies and Senior AdviserFollowing a Manila visit to see ASEAN leaders, hold the first Quad leaders’ summit since 2024, and meet with Philippine President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. that highlighted the Indo-Pacific’s continuing desire for U.S. engagement, President Trump’s participation in the Shenzhen APEC meetings was long on symbolism but short on tangible outcomes. Xi’s unprecedented airport greeting, mirroring President Trump’s September Washington welcome, showed an eagerness for a personal relationship with Trump that undercut arguments that Beijing now has the upper hand. Following announcement of a new U.S. rule targeting China’s remote access to U.S. semiconductors that previously might have led to Chinese retaliation, Xi instead cranked up the fanfare for Trump while the two punted trade issues to the December G20 meeting in Miami. The ballyhooed meeting between Trump, Xi, and Russian President Vladimir Putin ignored that only global victors can have a Yalta. Instead, the three face significant problems: Xi a stagnant Chinese economy, Putin having squandered Russia’s great power mojo in Ukraine, and Trump the worst midterm elections for his party in 50 years amid an Iran quagmire. The joint statement—rare for Trump—largely regurgitated existing documents but offered surprising language on future trilateral discussions on managing nuclear risks. While modest, this was a concession by China, which has long rejected trilateral arms control. Xi probably calculated hosting the meeting was worth this price, particularly as China continues its massive nuclear buildup. Trump believes friendliness with Putin and Xi will lead to future stability rather than embolden U.S. adversaries, ignoring the deep concerns of U.S. allies and partners that the meeting smacked of appeasement—not another Yalta, but a Munich without umbrellas. 

Image

Trump in Manila: Symbolism over SubstanceGregory B. Poling, Director and Senior Fellow, Southeast Asia Program and Asia Maritime Transparency InitiativePresident Trump arrived in Manila on the final day of the November 15–17 ASEAN and East Asia Summit meetings, missing the official multilaterals. He joined his counterparts from Australia, India, and Japan for the first in-person Quad leaders’ meeting of his second term before attending a dinner with Southeast Asian counterparts in lieu of the normal U.S.-ASEAN Summit. The itinerary also included bilateral engagements with Philippine President Marcos and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul. In each of these, symbolism trumped substance.In meeting with Marcos, Trump omitted any reference to the South China Sea disputes. When asked about the issue by a reporter, he replied, “I am not concerned about that at all, that would be taken care of,” which has sparked predictable unease in the Philippine press. Trump did insist the U.S.-Philippines alliance has “never been better” and a White House fact sheet pledged to “pursue” $2 billion in foreign military financing for the Philippines that Congress authorized last year. On trade, Trump and Anutin signed a joint statement on the “substantial conclusion” of negotiations for a U.S.-Thailand trade deal but admitted important details need to be worked out. Trump claimed the agreement would eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports to Thailand only to be immediately contradicted by Thailand’s commerce minister. Trump later announced that the United States and the Philippines had finalized their “biggest” trade deal ever. But Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez later told reporters, “There are really no details yet. It’s just generalities for now.”  

Image

China Flexing its Muscle Prior to APECBonny Lin, Director, China Power Project and Senior AdviserIn the lead-up to APEC from late October to early November, China heightened its military activities across the region and, in some cases, reversed trends from earlier this year. The most notable development was the likely coordinated maritime activity of Chinese naval vessels from three different People’s Liberation Army (PLA) theater commands in the Philippine Sea. This involved the Liaoning aircraft carrier and fifteen other People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) ships that formed four separate naval task forces in early November, representing one of the largest PLAN deployments beyond the First Island Chain. Around Taiwan, this included the highest level of “official ships”—China Coast Guard (CCG) or research vessels—in history, with a record 165 vessels operating around the island in October. November 2 saw one of this year’s highest numbers of PLA aircraft—49 sorties—detected around Taiwan. At the same time, around Japan, the Japanese Joint Staff reported 94 jet scrambles against PLA aircraft in October, the highest figure since November 2021. In mid-October, China revealed that a July 2026 ICBM launch was from one of its newest nuclear-powered submarines. There were also reports of China conducting a ballistic missile intercept test.This surge in the range of military activity—reaching over 100 PLAN and CCG vessels across the region on November 3, 2026, as reported by Taiwan—caused some to label it a silent, unnamed Chinese military exercise. However, it is not clear this was one big exercise. It was likely a series of separate Chinese military activities driven by a range of political motivations. What is clear, though, is that Beijing was not afraid to showcase and exercise its military might prior to APEC. 

Image

Takeaways from the Trilateral Summit’s Joint StatementThomas J. Christensen, Pritzker Chair in Geopolitics, CSIS; James T. Shotwell Professor of International Relations, Columbia University School of International and Public AffairsThe trilateral summit was hardly the Yalta 2.0 that U.S. allies and partners feared. The joint statement reflects no major agreements. Still, of concern to Ukraine, the call for freely flowing refined energy products suggests that the Trump administration might continue to suspend wartime sanctions on Russian exports of diesel.President Trump had prioritized nuclear arms control going into the summit, but there is currently no real prospect for trilateral arms limitations. Beijing is expanding its nuclear arsenal quickly and is unwilling to negotiate limitations while its nuclear stockpile is still a fraction of Washington’s and Moscow’s. So, the joint statement that “nuclear war cannot be won” should only be viewed as an intellectual prerequisite for any trilateral arms limitation talks that might occur in the distant future.The call for dialogues about limiting “nuclear risk” might contain more near-term value. In a world of artificial intelligence, automated weapons, and the proliferation of delivery systems that can deliver either conventional or nuclear ordnance, it seems prudent to hold meetings about ensuring human control of nuclear weapons and reducing the dangers of crisis escalation inherent in dual-use delivery systems.The jointly stated opposition to nuclear proliferation is hardly new. And it is highly unlikely that Russia or China will pressure Iran to surrender its nuclear material or North Korea to denuclearize. Instead, Beijing and Moscow are much more likely to frustrate the Trump administration by continuing to assist Tehran in resisting U.S. military and economic pressure. 

Image

Xi Gets a BoostBrian Hart, Executive Director, China Room, and Senior Fellow, Geopolitics and Foreign Policy DepartmentChina’s leader Xi Jinping got a boost at home from this week’s summitry. As host of the APEC summit, he seized every opportunity to raise his stature.Xi was undoubtedly wary of the risks of holding a trilateral meeting with President Trump and President Putin, but it did offer him something important: global headlines of himself “chairing” their “groundbreaking” meeting, flanked by the U.S. and Russian leaders. The imagery echoes China’s 2025 Victory Day Parade, when Xi was pictured center stage with Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un at his side. Xi is rumored to have left the parade pleased that he had shown himself and China as the leader of the Global South. He is likely leaving this week’s meetings with renewed confidence in his and China’s status.Adding to his spoils, the summit’s host city, Shenzhen, bears personal significance for Xi. His father, Xi Zhongxun, was instrumental in building up Shenzhen from a small village into a sprawling technology hub. In gathering world leaders there, Xi demonstrated how he is continuing to transform the country and building on his father’s work.These symbolic wins are not trivial for Xi. He has staked his legacy on making China strong on the world stage. Xi has asserted his place in China’s history by suggesting that China stood up under Mao Zedong, got rich under Deng Xiaoping, and is growing strong under his rule. High-profile moments like these allow Xi to portray China as powerful and respected under his leadership. 

Image

Trilateral Nuclear Dialogues Present New Opportunities for ProgressJoseph Rodgers, Deputy Director and Senior Fellow, Project on Nuclear IssuesIn the Kylin Villa statement, the United States, Russia, and China agreed that a nuclear war can never be won and must never be fought, while committing to a new trilateral dialogue on nuclear risk reduction and nonproliferation. The vow that nuclear war must never be fought is a familiar maxim of nuclear arms control diplomacy, but the formation of this dialogue on nuclear issues is novel.This marks the first time that a Chinese president has personally committed to Beijing’s participation in nuclear risk reduction. While the statement itself is not groundbreaking, leader-level pronouncements provide critical political cover and inertia for officials across the three governments to secure budgets and institutional support for sustained talks. Beijing has traditionally remained wary of nuclear discussions, claiming that the Chinese arsenal lacks parity with Washington and Moscow. This high-level push could open doors inside the Chinese bureaucracy, possibly making progress on arms control more achievable.To succeed, this dialogue should prioritize pragmatic discussions over an unattainable arms-control agenda. On risk reduction, negotiators should focus on three concrete areas: (1) identifying incentives for nuclear use through discussions about military doctrines, (2) codifying a trilateral commitment that nuclear weapons will never be launched by artificial intelligence, and (3) conducting reciprocal visits at nuclear sites to build working-level trust over arms control verification technologies. On nonproliferation, the discussions should focus on Iran’s nuclear program, strengthening the Treaty on the Nonproliferation of Nuclear Weapons, and managing proliferation pressures from emerging technologies such as modern reactor designs and new uranium enrichment and plutonium reprocessing methods. 

Image

Putin’s Yalta 2.0 Fantasy: Running on EmptyThomas Glynn Hanley, Deputy Director and Fellow, Europe, Russia, and Eurasia ProgramPresident Putin may think he’s the latest in a long line of Russian strongmen, but the Russia he led to Yalta 2.0 in Shenzhen is far weaker than the Soviet Union that hosted the original in 1945. The U.S. and Chinese economies are roughly 11 and 7.5 times larger than Russia’s. Sitting as an equal beside Trump and Xi is a win for Putin, the stuff of KGB dreams.The leaders’ “Declaration towards Peace” offered the obligatory nod to fighting global challenges. But it also pledged to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” Russia has historically been the third-largest refiner after the United States and China, but it will be hard-pressed to deliver on that pledge.Ukrainian drone strikes dropped Russian refinery throughput, the amount of crude oil its refineries actually process, to its lowest level in more than 20 years this summer, and a renewed campaign has cut it by as much as 45 percent since late October. The strikes increasingly hit complex secondary refining units, which can take six to eight months to repair and are essential to producing gasoline and diesel. To make matters worse for Moscow, Western sanctions restrict its access to replacement equipment. Rosneft, Russia’s largest oil company, is delaying repairs while it waits on Russian-made copies or Chinese imports that can take months to arrive and may not even fit the damaged machinery. Moscow has had to ban gasoline and most diesel exports, ration fuel at home, and import petrol at record levels.But the pledge may also carry a darker message. President Trump has already pushed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop striking Russian refineries, which he says is “hurting the world.” The joint promise to boost fuel supplies suggests Washington will keep pressing Kyiv to spare the very facilities that power Moscow’s war machine.  

Image

Two Summits in Asia: One That Should Have Delivered, One That Never CouldAman Thakker, Fellow, Chair on India and Emerging Asia EconomicsPresident Trump revived the Quad during his first term after nearly a decade of dormancy. His second term has told a different story. After tariff disputes and friction over India’s Russian oil purchases strained U.S.-India ties in 2025, a planned leaders’ summit India was slated to host never materialized, resulting in a two-year gap of a meeting of the Quad leaders—the longest since its revival and subsequent elevation to the leaders’ level in 2021.When the four leaders finally reassembled this week in Manila, it presented a real opportunity to translate alignment between Quad governments into concrete deliverables. Instead, this week’s split-screen of President Trump at two dramatically different summits—one with long-standing allies and partners in Australia, Japan, and India, and the other with Russia and China—exemplified a gap that defined President Trump’s week in Asia: a summit that should have delivered and did not, paired with one that, despite all its fanfare, never could.The Quad can still deliver, but only if it trades the priorities of a decade ago for those of today. The Quad announced one fully operational output on maritime domain awareness, reflecting priorities set in 2017, when Chinese maritime activity was the central worry in the Indo-Pacific. The strategic landscape has since shifted to who sets the rules for frontier AI, controls critical semiconductor and critical minerals supply choke points, and can defend against machine-speed cyberattacks. The newly announced Quad Business Leaders’ Forum, set to convene in Mumbai for the first time in 2027, offers one vehicle for this reorientation. However, until the Quad treats these emerging priorities as its core business, it will remain a grouping that reaffirms its relevance each time leaders meet, rather than one that delivers. 

Image

Shifting the Focus from Trade Barriers to Trade EnablersRomina Bandura, Senior Fellow, Economic Development and Prosperity ProgramRecent U.S. economic statecraft has been dominated by tariffs and export controls, which were a main topic of discussion during President Trump’s visit to China. These defensive tools, or “sticks,” can only do so much to position the United States as a global economic powerhouse and trade partner of choice for countries. Some countries are using trade infrastructure, especially ports, as “carrots”—strategic assets to either weaponize supply chains or enable their flow. Nowhere is this more important than exporting critical supplies such as food through ports in the Black Sea and energy through ports near the Strait of Hormuz. This issue went missing during the Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral meeting.As the world’s second-largest trading nation after China, the United States depends on a global network of overseas commercial ports to enable both trade and military operations. However, the United States remains behind; it has a limited footprint in global commercial port infrastructure, particularly in container terminals. U.S. adversaries are using port infrastructure to serve their own economic and foreign policy interests. The United States has important comparative advantages across the port ecosystem to offer countries, including in engineering and design, marine construction, customs and security systems, cybersecurity, transparent concession governance, and financing. Overseas ports deserve more U.S. attention if the country wants to remain an economic powerhouse, be a better partner to other countries, and mitigate economic, geopolitical, and security vulnerabilities arising from trade dependencies. The focus has to shift from imposing trade barriers to offering trade enablers. Ports are an important part of that discussion. 

Image

Fentanyl Becomes a Regular ItemStephen Morrison, Senior Vice President and Director, Global Health Policy Center, and Michaela Simoneau, Fellow, Global Health Policy CenterShenzhen is now the fourth consecutive Trump-Xi summit at which fentanyl has figured as a priority topic. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs reports that President Trump was positive about the results of U.S.-China cooperation to control fentanyl and its chemical precursors, and that President Xi called for more cooperation. A pattern appears to be emerging.There are strong motivations for both governments to work actively on counternarcotics efforts. Professionals in both countries have achieved surprisingly productive cooperation in drug-trafficking investigations, operations, prosecution, extradition, and export controls, with high-level coordination among ministerial officials. It is innately a good news story for both governments: Lives lost to fentanyl overdoses in the United States have dropped by 50 percent since 2022. The Trump administration has maintained a 10 percent fentanyl tariff to push for more aggressive Chinese action. Even so, the “constructive strategic stability” forged since the countries’ trade truce has opened the way for this form of health security cooperation that brings mutual benefits. President Xi highlighted joint action on healthy aging as another potential regional priority in his APEC remarks.Stay tuned for what transpires at the G20 summit in Miami this December, when Presidents Trump and Xi are expected to meet again. The United States may use the G20 chair to advocate for a stronger global response to the highly dangerous Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as it did at ministerial meetings in September and October. Total U.S. pledges to support the Ebola response now amount to $887 million of the over $2 billion committed globally. China’s $18 million in pledges are much more modest, but important nonetheless. As with the U.S.-China dialogue on fentanyl, a surprising pattern seems to be emerging of U.S. multilateral leadership that brings China into the fold to battle transnational health threats.
